opus-5.5.text:
I see these three things as deeply connected, and honestly, I think the connection gets overlooked because the dominant narrative in the field has been "bigger is better" for quite a few years now.

Start with sustainability. When we've measured the energy and carbon footprint of models, and I've done a lot of that work, including looking at the full life cycle from training through deployment, what jumps out is that the costs scale dramatically with size. And it's not just training. Inference, the day-to-day use of these models, can end up dwarfing training costs once a model is deployed to millions of users. So when we default to a giant general-purpose model for a task that a much smaller, task-specific model could handle, like classifying text or answering questions about a specific domain, we're burning a lot of energy for very marginal or sometimes no gains in performance. Smaller models are one of the most direct levers we have for reducing AI's environmental impact.

Then there's equity, and it ties in really naturally. If the only models that count as state of the art require thousands of GPUs and tens of millions of dollars to train, then you've basically decided who gets to participate in AI research and development: a handful of very large companies in a handful of countries. Researchers at universities, people in the Global South, small startups, nonprofits, communities who want to build tools in their own languages, they're all shut out. Smaller models that can run on modest hardware, or even on a laptop or a phone, open the door for many more people to build, study, audit, and adapt these systems. That's a power question as much as a technical one.

There's also an equity dimension to the environmental piece itself. The communities that bear the brunt of climate change, and of things like data center water usage or the strain on local power grids, are often not the ones benefiting most from these technologies. So the environmental cost isn't evenly distributed either.

And I'd add transparency to the mix. Smaller, open models are much easier to scrutinize. You can actually examine them, evaluate them for bias, understand their behavior. With huge closed models, we often don't even know basic information like how much energy they use, which makes accountability really hard.

So for me, advocating for smaller models isn't about being anti-progress. It's about asking: what's the right tool for the job? If we started from that question instead of reflexively reaching for the biggest model available, we'd end up with AI that's more sustainable, more accessible, and more accountable. Those goals reinforce each other rather than being trade-offs.

r001.rationale: It says smaller models on modest hardware let many more people build, study, audit, and adapt AI systems, making AI more accessible.

r002.rationale: It explicitly frames broader access to smaller models as a power question, explaining that they let people outside dominant companies participate in AI development.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so for me those three things are really deeply connected, and I think people often treat them as separate conversations when they're actually the same conversation.

So the sustainability piece is the one I've been working on the longest. When I started looking at the carbon footprint of machine learning, it was really about training, right? These huge models, these huge training runs, how much energy they use, how much carbon they emit. And that's still important. But what I've realized over the past few years is that deployment is actually where a lot of the impact happens. Because you train a model once, but then you run it millions or billions of times. And so if you have a model that's ten or a hundred times bigger than it needs to be for the task, you're paying that cost every single time someone sends a query. We did a study a while back comparing, say, a task-specific model for sentiment analysis or question answering versus a general-purpose large model doing the same task, and the difference in energy was orders of magnitude. And the big model wasn't necessarily better at the task. So from a pure sustainability standpoint, smaller, more specialized models just make sense. You're not using a sledgehammer to crack a nut.

But then the equity piece comes in, and this is where it gets interesting to me. Because who gets to train and run the biggest models? It's a handful of companies, mostly in the US, with access to tens of thousands of GPUs. If you're a researcher in a university lab, or a startup, or an organization in the Global South, you can't participate in that. You can't train those models, often you can't even run them, and in many cases you can't even audit them because they're behind an API. So the whole trajectory of "bigger is better" is also a trajectory of concentration of power. It concentrates who gets to build AI, who gets to study it, who gets to decide what it's used for. And smaller models kind of push back on that. If a model fits on a laptop, or on a single consumer GPU, then a lot more people can fine-tune it, inspect it, adapt it to their language or their context, and that's a real democratization story, not just a marketing one.

And then there's a more subtle equity dimension around where the environmental costs land. Data centers get built where energy and water are cheap, and that's often in communities that don't benefit from the AI systems being trained there. So the footprint isn't evenly distributed. The people reaping the benefits of these giant models and the people bearing the costs, whether that's water usage or grid strain or the mining for the hardware, are often not the same people. So when I talk about sustainability, I'm not just talking about a global CO2 number. I'm talking about justice, essentially.

So in my mind, smaller models are kind of a lever that moves all three of those things at once. They lower the environmental cost, they widen access, and they make the systems more transparent and more accountable. And the thing I always push back on is this framing that we have to choose, that you either get capability or you get sustainability and equity. I really don't think that's true for most real-world use cases. Most of what people actually need AI for doesn't require a trillion-parameter model. The trick is building the incentives and the measurement tools so that people actually choose the right-sized model instead of defaulting to the biggest one because it's what's in the headlines.

r001.rationale: It says smaller models let more people fine-tune, inspect, and adapt AI, calling this a democratization of access.

r002.rationale: It says smaller models push back against concentrated power by enabling more people to build and study AI and decide how it is used.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re closely connected, because the resources needed to build and run AI affect both its environmental footprint and who gets to participate. If using AI requires enormous amounts of compute, then you’re excluding people and organizations that don’t have access to that infrastructure or the money to pay for it.

Smaller models can help lower those barriers. They can require less energy to run and be easier to adapt to a particular task or deploy on local hardware. That can give communities more control over their data and over what they want the technology to do.

But smaller doesn’t automatically mean sustainable or equitable. You still have to ask how often a model is being used, what hardware it runs on, whose needs it serves, and how well it works for different languages and communities. A small model that performs poorly for the people using it isn’t solving the equity problem.

So I’d start with the need: What are we trying to accomplish, and what resources are actually necessary? Sometimes a smaller, specialized model is enough. Sometimes you don’t need AI at all. Making room for those choices is an important part of connecting sustainability with equity.

r001.rationale: The response says smaller models can lower resource and cost barriers, making AI more accessible to people and organizations without large compute infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It connects smaller, locally deployable models with communities gaining more control over their data and how the technology is used, expressing a shift in who holds power.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as closely connected. When we talk about sustainability, we often focus on the energy used to train a model. But we also need to think about what happens every time someone uses it. If a smaller model can do the task you need, using a much larger one can add computational cost without adding much value.

That’s also an equity issue. If building and running AI requires enormous amounts of computing power, participation is limited to organizations that can afford it. Smaller models can make it easier for researchers and communities to adapt systems to their own needs, including working with their own languages and running them on hardware they actually have access to.

But smaller doesn’t automatically mean sustainable or equitable. You still have to ask how well the model works, whose needs it serves, and who bears the costs. For me, the goal is to choose an appropriate tool for a particular need, and to make those decisions with the people who will be affected.

r001.rationale: It says smaller models make it easier for researchers and communities to adapt AI to their needs and run it on available hardware, broadening access.

r002.rationale: It contrasts compute access limited to organizations that can afford it with smaller models enabling researchers and communities to participate and shape systems for their own needs, describing a broader distribution of agency in AI.
